analysis.one_liner: Bars dealers from selling or renting used cars with unfixed safety recalls until repairs are made.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced in May 2021 with three Democratic senators behind it, it was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it illegal for a dealer to sell, lease, or loan a used car to a consumer until any open safety recall on that vehicle had been repaired. It applied to anyone selling at least five vehicles a year, with exceptions for wholesale sales, junk cars, and cases where recall information was not available. To keep dealers from being stuck with unfixable cars, it required manufacturers to pay dealers at least 1% of a vehicle's fair-market value per month if the manufacturer failed to make a repair available within 60 days. The bill never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Used-car buyers, lessees, and rental customers gain: they could no longer be sold or handed a vehicle with an unfixed safety recall. NHTSA recall data has repeatedly shown tens of millions of vehicles on the road with open recalls, and a buyer of a recalled used car typically has no easy way to know the defect exists or to get it fixed free. Road users generally also benefit from fewer defective vehicles in circulation.

how_it_helps.text: A dealer could not sell, lease, or loan a used car to a consumer until its safety recall defect was fixed, so buyers would no longer unknowingly purchase a car with an open recall.

Dealers would be paid at least 1% of a vehicle's fair-market value per month if the manufacturer fails to make a repair available within 60 days, up to the vehicle's full value — preventing dealers from bearing the cost of manufacturer delays.
Exceptions protect against edge cases: wholesale sales, junk vehicles reported to the national title database, and sales where recall information was genuinely unavailable from official sources.

analysis.who_pays: Auto dealers bear the direct cost: they must check recall status and hold vehicles until repairs are made, and cannot pass unfixable cars to consumers. Auto manufacturers bear the reimbursement obligation — at least 1% of a vehicle's value per month — when they fail to make a recall remedy available within 60 days. Those manufacturer costs could be passed on in vehicle prices. Consumers face no direct cost.

drawbacks.text: The ban applies to any dealer selling at least five vehicles in a year, so small independent used-car lots carry compliance burdens (checking recall status, holding vehicles) alongside large franchise dealers.

If a manufacturer cannot or will not supply a repair, a dealer must either sit on the vehicle or sell it only at wholesale — and while the bill pays dealers for waiting, those storage and financing costs still flow into used-car inventory and prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and focused: closing a known gap that lets dealers sell cars with unfixed safety defects, which protects used-car buyers and everyone else on the road. The costs are modest and the bill tries to cover them — dealers are compensated (at least 1% of a vehicle's value per month) if a manufacturer drags its feet on a repair, and the ban has carve-outs for wholesale sales, junk cars, and cases where recall information was genuinely unavailable. The main good-faith objection is that the compliance burden falls on dealers, including small ones selling as few as five vehicles a year, and that some manufacturers are slow to produce replacement parts for older recalled vehicles — but the bill responds to exactly that with the dealer reimbursement and a one-year lead time before taking effect. On balance, the protections outweigh the burdens.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in May 2021, no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened, and it died when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Blumenthal introduced the bill on May 26, 2021, with Markey and Warren as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day — the only action the bill ever received.
No further action appears in the record through the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Used-car dealers can continue selling and renting vehicles with open safety recalls, and manufacturers face no new penalty for slow recall repairs.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Senate Commerce Committee, where the bill sat, never took it up.

industries.industry: Used car and franchise auto dealers
industries.note: The bill blocks dealers from selling or renting recalled vehicles to consumers until repairs are made, but pays dealers at least 1% of a vehicle's value per month when a manufacturer is slow to supply the fix. For most dealers this is a modest compliance burden in exchange for not selling defective cars.

Manufacturers would face financial penalties for failing to make recall repairs available to dealers within 60 days, creating direct cost pressure to fix recalls faster and to keep parts flowing for older vehicles.

Rental fleets loan vehicles to consumers, so open-recall cars could no longer be rented out, requiring fleets to track and repair recalls before renting. Rental customers gain the same protection as used-car buyers.
